title: What exactly happens when two transactions deadlock (A locks row 1 then waits for row 2 while B locks row 2 then waits for row 1), how does InnoDB handle it (it detects the cycle and rolls back one transaction as the victim), and why must the application be ready to RETRY the rolled-back transaction — plus how do you reduce deadlocks (consistent lock ordering, short transactions, proper indexing to lock fewer rows) rather than claiming "deadlocks should never happen"?
shortTitle: Deadlocks — What Happens, How InnoDB Handles Them, and Why You Must Retry

s1_definition.profdef: A deadlock is a circular wait: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and waits for row 2, while transaction B holds a lock on row 2 and waits for row 1, so neither can proceed and neither will ever release its lock. InnoDB detects the cycle in its wait-for graph and breaks it by rolling back one transaction (the victim), returning an error; the surviving transaction completes. The application must be prepared to catch the deadlock error and retry the rolled-back transaction, because deadlocks are a normal, expected outcome under concurrency, not a bug to be eliminated entirely.
s1_definition.analogy: Two National Bank of India clerks each grab one of two ledgers the other needs: clerk A holds the savings ledger and reaches for the loan ledger, while clerk B holds the loan ledger and reaches for the savings ledger. Both are now frozen, each waiting for what the other holds. A supervisor (InnoDB) spots this standoff, tells one clerk "drop everything and start over" (rolls back the victim), which frees a ledger so the other finishes. The clerk who was sent back must simply try the whole task again — that retry is normal, not a sign anything is broken.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A deadlock is a circular wait: transaction A holds a lock on row 1 and waits for row 2, while transaction B holds a lock on row 2 and waits for row 1, so neither can proceed and neither will ever release its lock. InnoDB detects the cycle in its wait-for graph and breaks it by rolling back one transaction (the victim), returning an error; the surviving transaction completes. The application must be prepared to catch the deadlock error and retry the rolled-back transaction, because deadlocks are a normal, expected outcome under concurrency, not a bug to be eliminated entirely.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two National Bank of India clerks each grab one of two ledgers the other needs: clerk A holds the savings ledger and reaches for the loan ledger, while clerk B holds the loan ledger and reaches for the savings ledger. Both are now frozen, each waiting for what the other holds. A supervisor (InnoDB) spots this standoff, tells one clerk "drop everything and start over" (rolls back the victim), which frees a ledger so the other finishes. The clerk who was sent back must simply try the whole task again — that retry is normal, not a sign anything is broken.

**One line to remember:** A deadlock is a circular lock wait; InnoDB detects the cycle and rolls back one transaction as the victim, so the application must catch the error and retry — and you reduce deadlocks with consistent lock ordering, short transactions, and good indexing, not by pretending they never happen.

sections.s2_technical:
A deadlock arises from a specific sequence under row locking. Transaction A acquires an exclusive lock on row 1 and then requests row 2; transaction B has already acquired row 2 and then requests row 1. A waits for B to release row 2, and B waits for A to release row 1 — a cycle in the "who waits for whom" (wait-for) graph. Without intervention both would wait forever. This is distinct from simple lock contention, where one transaction merely waits and then proceeds once the other commits; a deadlock is a mutual, unbreakable wait.

InnoDB maintains a wait-for graph and runs automatic deadlock detection. When it finds a cycle, it immediately chooses a victim — typically the transaction that has done the least work (fewest rows modified, so it is cheapest to undo) — rolls it back entirely, releases its locks, and returns error 1213, "Deadlock found when trying to get lock." The other transaction in the cycle then acquires the freed lock and proceeds. InnoDB also has an innodb_lock_wait_timeout as a fallback for cases detection doesn't cover (such as locks across engines), after which a waiting statement is aborted. The key point is that the database resolves the deadlock automatically and quickly; it does not hang.

Because the victim's transaction is rolled back, the application must be ready to retry it. The correct pattern is to catch the deadlock error (SQLState 40001 / MySQL error 1213) and re-run the whole transaction, usually a small bounded number of times with a short, slightly randomized backoff to avoid immediately re-colliding. Retrying is safe only if the transaction is written to be idempotent or fully re-runnable from the start, which is why you keep all its logic inside the transaction boundary. Claiming "deadlocks should never happen" is wrong: under real concurrency they are an expected, well-handled event, and robust systems treat them as a normal retryable condition.

That said, you reduce their frequency. The single most effective technique is consistent lock ordering: if every transaction always locks resources in the same global order (for example, always lock the lower account id before the higher), the circular wait cannot form. Keeping transactions short minimizes the window in which locks are held, reducing the chance of overlap. Proper indexing ensures a statement locks only the few rows it needs via an index seek instead of scanning and locking many rows, which both lowers contention and avoids locking unrelated rows. Other measures are using a lower isolation level where correctness allows (fewer gap/next-key locks), accessing tables in a consistent order, and batching large operations. The senior framing is a two-part answer: design to make deadlocks rare (ordering, short transactions, indexing) and design to survive the ones that still occur (detect the error and retry) — never assume they are impossible.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem — National Bank of India's transfer service deadlocked intermittently: a transfer from account 1 to account 2 locked account 1 then account 2, while a simultaneous transfer from account 2 to account 1 locked account 2 then account 1, forming a cycle. InnoDB rolled one back with error 1213, but the application had no retry and surfaced a raw failure to the customer. The fix was two-fold: always lock the two accounts in a consistent order (lower id first) so the cycle cannot form, and wrap the transfer in a bounded retry so any residual deadlock is transparently re-attempted.

Our mini-project simulates two concurrent cross-transfers: a naive version that locks in request order (and can deadlock) and a fixed version that locks accounts in a consistent order (eliminating the cycle), plus a retry wrapper that re-runs a victimized transaction — demonstrating detection, the victim rollback, ordered locking, and retry.
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: two accounts, account 1 and account 2, each with one thousand, with two opposing transfers running at the same time.

Step 1 — With naive locking, a transfer from account 1 to account 2 would lock account 1 first, and the opposing transfer from account 2 to account 1 would lock account 2 first; each then waits for the other's held account, forming the circular wait that is a deadlock.

Step 2 — With ordered locking, both transfers compute a consistent order and always lock the lower account id (account 1) before the higher (account 2), regardless of the transfer's direction. The second transfer therefore waits for account 1 at the very first step rather than after already holding account 2, so no cycle can form.

Step 3 — Because the cycle cannot form, one transfer completes fully and releases both locks, then the other proceeds and completes; both balances settle correctly and neither thread is stuck, demonstrating that consistent lock ordering structurally prevents the deadlock.

Step 4 — The retry wrapper models a residual deadlock: a transaction runs, the simulated engine reports it as the victim with error 1213 on the first attempt, the wrapper catches it, waits a short randomized backoff, and re-runs the whole transaction.

Step 5 — The second attempt succeeds, so the wrapper reports two attempts and final success, showing that treating a deadlock as a normal retryable condition — rather than a fatal error surfaced to the customer — makes the system robust.

Final output:

```text
Ordered locking: a1=1000 a2=1000  (completed, no deadlock)
Retry wrapper: attempts=2 finalSuccess=true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  DEADLOCK (naive order):
    A: lock row1 ──wait──▶ row2 (held by B)
    B: lock row2 ──wait──▶ row1 (held by A)      cycle → neither proceeds
         │ InnoDB detects cycle in wait-for graph
         ▼ roll back VICTIM (least work) → error 1213 → other proceeds
    app: catch 1213 ─▶ backoff ─▶ RETRY whole txn

  PREVENTION (ordered):
    both always lock lower-id first → no cycle can form
    + short transactions + indexed predicates (lock fewer rows)
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Make Deadlocks Rare AND Survivable ═══

  ┌──────────────┐  transfer   ┌───────────────────────┐  ordered locks  ┌──────────┐
  │ Transfer API │ ──────────▶ │ TransferService        │ ──────────────▶ │ accounts │
  │ (retry wrap) │             │ lock lower-id first    │                 │  rows    │
  └──────────────┘             └───────────────────────┘                 └──────────┘
        ▲ catch 1213 → backoff → retry          │ InnoDB: detect cycle → victim rollback
        └────────────────────────────────────────┘
  Rare:  consistent lock order • short txns • indexes (fewer locked rows)
  Survive: detect deadlock error (40001/1213) → bounded retry with backoff
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Ordered Locking + Retry ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Resource Ordering: global lock order breaks the cycle             │
  │ Retry/Circuit: bounded re-attempt with backoff                    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: service transfers; wrapper handles retry                      │
  │ O: new retry policy = new wrapper, txn unchanged                 │
  │ D: txn passed as Runnable, re-runnable from start                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Deadlock anatomy & handling ──
  CAUSE   : circular wait (A:row1→row2, B:row2→row1)
  DETECT  : InnoDB wait-for graph → pick VICTIM (least work) → rollback → error 1213
  FALLBACK: innodb_lock_wait_timeout aborts long waiters
  RETRY   : catch 40001/1213 → backoff (randomized) → re-run (bounded attempts)
  REDUCE  : consistent lock order | short txns | index predicates | lower isolation

  ── Call Chain ──
  1. Demo.main()
  2.   → transferOrdered(a1,a2) & transferOrdered(a2,a1)  [lower id first → no cycle]
  3.   → withRetry(txn, 3)  [attempt1: 1213 victim → backoff → attempt2 success]
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A deadlock is a circular wait between transactions: transaction A holds an exclusive lock on row 1 and requests row 2, while transaction B holds row 2 and requests row 1, so A waits for B and B waits for A, forming a cycle in the wait-for graph that neither can escape on its own. This is different from ordinary contention, where a transaction simply waits and then proceeds; a deadlock is a mutual, unbreakable standoff. InnoDB handles it automatically: it maintains a wait-for graph, detects the cycle, and immediately rolls back one transaction as the victim — typically the one that has done the least work and is cheapest to undo — releasing its locks and returning error 1213, "Deadlock found when trying to get lock," so the surviving transaction acquires the freed lock and completes. There is also innodb_lock_wait_timeout as a fallback for waits detection doesn't cover.

Because the victim is rolled back, the application must be ready to retry: the correct pattern is to catch the deadlock error, SQLState 40001 or MySQL error 1213, and re-run the whole transaction a small bounded number of times with a short randomized backoff so it doesn't immediately re-collide, which is safe only because the transaction is written to be fully re-runnable from the start. I never claim "deadlocks should never happen" — under real concurrency they are an expected, well-handled event, and robust systems treat them as a normal retryable condition. At the National Bank of India our transfer service deadlocked when opposing transfers locked the same two accounts in opposite order, and InnoDB rolled one back but we had no retry, so a raw failure reached the customer. We fixed it two ways: we made every transfer lock the two accounts in a consistent order, always the lower account id first, so the cycle can no longer form, and we wrapped the transfer in a bounded retry so any residual deadlock is transparently re-attempted. To reduce deadlocks generally I use consistent lock ordering as the most effective technique, keep transactions short to shrink the window locks are held, and index predicates so a statement locks only the few rows it needs instead of scanning and locking many. The line I always state is that a deadlock is a circular lock wait that InnoDB resolves by rolling back a victim, so the application must catch the error and retry, and you reduce deadlocks with consistent lock ordering, short transactions, and good indexing rather than pretending they never occur.
